provenance: H M King Edward VII (d.1910). | By descent to H M King George V (d.1936). | Acquired by William Berry, 1st Viscount Camrose (1879-1954) see footnote below. | By descent to Seymour Berry, 2nd Viscount Camrose (1909-1995). | Christie's Hackwood auction, lot 125 20th April 1998. | Property of a Gentleman. | | History | H.M.Y. Britannia was ordered in 1892 by the Prince of Wales, later Edward VII and after his death owned by George V. Designed by G L Watson and launched in 1893 her early career was remarkably successful. | | In 1921, her new owner, George V was keen to start big class yacht racing again and Britannia was fitted out accordingly and for the first few seasons she was highly successful though as the years progressed, she was more unable to hold her own against the bigger J-class racing yachts of more modern rig. Although converted to Bermuda rig in 1931 she was withdrawn from racing having sailed a total of 635 races, winning 231 first prizes and 129 second and third. | | King George V's dying wish was for his beloved yacht to follow him to the grave. On 10 July 1936, after Britannia had been stripped of her spars and fittings which were subsequently sold at auction, her hull was towed out to St Catherine's Deep near the Isle of Wight, and she was sunk by H.M.S. Winchester. | | It was from this auction that William Berry, the newspaper magnate, acquired this gangway door. | | William Berry, Ist Viscount Camrose (1879-1954) and his son were both keen yachtsmen. Elected a member of the Squadron in 1930, he competed in his yacht Cambria in the large class for boats over 20m in length. In 1930, the year of the Admirals Cup challenge, Cambria lost to the eventual British entry Sir Thomas Lipton's Shamrock V in a special race organised by the Squadron.

provenance: Anon. sale, Christie's, London, 30 January 1970, lot 90A. | With Richard Green, London. | Private collection, UK (purchased from the above in 1976). | Thence by descent to the current owner. | | The raison d'être for the American War of Independence was to free the thirteen colonies skirting the Atlantic coast of North America from British colonial rule. As had happened a generation earlier however, during the Seven Years' War (1756-63), the struggle soon widened into a much greater global battle between England and France, the latter having allied herself to the fledgling republic of the United States in the hope of making territorial gains at Britain's expense. One of the main arenas for this world-wide conflict was India and nowhere was there more activity than off the eastern coasts of the sub-continent and Ceylon. | | The English and French naval forces in Indian waters were surprisingly well-matched and, commanded by Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Hughes and Admiral Pierre André de Suffren respectively, the two fleets fought each other on no less than four occasions during the course of 1782. The first encounter, off Madras on 17th February, was bloody though indecisive, as were those on 12th April (off Providien, Ceylon) and 6th July (off Negapatam). The final action of the year, on 3rd September, was fought off Trincomalee, Ceylon, and whilst Hughes was subsequently criticised for not pressing home his initial advantage, the battle was seen as a British success and Suffren was forced to run into Trincomalee to escape the approaching monsoon. In every respect, Hughes's campaign was extremely successful and although Superb was lost off Bombay in 1783, Hughes eventually returned to England in triumph in 1785, after the Peace of Paris had been concluded. | | Once Hughes was back home, he commissioned Dominic Serres to portray his several victories in the East in a splendid series of great battle paintings which, in fact, proved to be the artist's last flirtation with works depicting large-scale naval actions, the genre for which he was justly famous. In addition to these battle pictures however, is this altogether calmer work, showing Hughes's squadron heaving-to in Table Bay, off Cape Town, where it would undoubtedly take on food and water whilst heading for the East Indies in the early summer of 1779.

artwork_title: View of Dublin Bay from the rocks between Salthill and Seapoint Stations
provenance: Anon. sale, Sotheby's, London, 6 May 2010, lot 3. | With Richard Green, London., stock no. BG 204 MS. | | Exhibited | Dublin, Royal Hibernian Academy, 1869, no. 156. | | The present work offers an important view of Dublin Bay in the late 1860s, seen from Seapoint Station looking towards the West Pier at Dún Laoghaire. Beechey demonstrates a keen sensitivity to both atmosphere and narrative, animating the shoreline with figures engaged in quiet, everyday activities. Groups of women gather among the rocks, some reading, others seated in conversation while nearby children play. At the water's edge, a small group of boys fish, lending a further note of liveliness to the scene. | | The bay itself is also alive with activity. Sailing and fishing vessels travel across the water, a rowing boat carries passengers, and a lone canoeist paddles gently. Steamships pass along the horizon, while the masts of tall ships rise behind the West Pier, reflecting the harbour's enduring role at the heart of the city's maritime activity. | | Perhaps the most notable feature in the painting is the inclusion of the recently completed rail infrastructure at Seapoint, dating to 1862. A train passes beneath the footbridge, steam billowing from its engine, while another is visible in the distance. Both subtle yet powerful markers of Dublin's modernisation. On the horizon stands the Salthill Hotel, accompanied by a row of Georgian houses that remain a recognisable feature of the landscape today. | | Richard Beechey, son of the distinguished artist Sir William Beechey R.A. and Lady Beechey, herself an accomplished miniaturist, pursued a career as both a naval officer and marine painter. Entering the Royal Navy at the age of fourteen, he rose to the rank of Admiral, at the same time developing his artistic talents and a reputation for his depictions of ships, often set against dramatic landscapes. Though English by birth, Beechey settled in Monkstown, County Dublin, following his marriage, and spent considerable time painting along the Irish coast. After retiring from naval service in 1864, he turned his attention increasingly to painting coastal views and scenes of daily life in the Dublin area, of which the present work is a particularly fine example.

provenance: Private collection, UK. | | The so-called Battle of the Nile was fought in Aboukir Bay, about 15 miles west of Alexandria, on 1 August 1798. Nelson, having spent most of the summer cruising the Eastern Mediterranean looking for Admiral Brueys' Toulon fleet, finally came upon it as it lay at anchor in Aboukir Bay following the disembarkation of the army with which Napoleon was to conquer Egypt. Brueys had chosen a strong position in a well-protected anchorage although Nelson had the advantage of surprise. More significantly, it was already six o'clock in the evening when Nelson sighted the French and, with only two hours of daylight remaining, Brueys was confident that any attack would have to be postponed until the next day, by which time his own fleet would be ready. Nelson, with typical daring, amazed both his own captains as well as the French by ordering his ships into the Bay where they engaged the enemy in a spirited action which lasted almost through the night. The decisive moment came just after 10 o'clock when the French flagship, the huge 120-gun L'Orient, blew up with a tremendous explosion and, when dawn broke, the French annihilation became apparent with nine of their badly damaged ships captured and another four destroyed. It was a glorious victory for Nelson, one of the greatest in British naval history, and the one which brought him to the pinnacle of his career. | | It is well-documented that Luny painted numerous versions of the battle of the Nile in the years immediately following it and, given that both of the works offered here depict the exploits of H.M.S. Zealous, it seems very probable they were commissioned by Captain Samuel Hood, his command during the epic engagement. H.M.S. Zealous was a 74-gun third rate built at Deptford and completed for sea in 1785. Despite this, she did not enter service until the War with Revolutionary France began and her first commission, under Captain James Young, was to the Mediterranean as flagship to Admiral Mason. By the time she had joined Nelson's fleet, she was commanded by Captain Samuel Hood and fought with great distinction at the Nile. She then remained in continuous service for the rest of the Napoleonic War until broken up in 1816.

provenance: Anon. sale, Sotheby's, London, 20 January 1993, lot 68. | Thomas James Perkins (1932–2016), Belvedere, California (acquired from the above). | Private collection, Tiburon, California (acquired from the above by bequest). | | Exhibited | Royal National Lifeboat Institution. | | When an unknown yacht from the United States won the brand-new 100 guinea cup at Cowes in August 1851, the yachting establishment was utterly ignorant of the fact that the trophy itself would soon assume the name of the 'America's Cup' and the challenges for it would ultimately become the world's most prestigious yacht races. Similarly, when the New York Yacht Club accepted the trophy for safe-keeping that same autumn, the men who had won it were equally unaware that American yachts would henceforward dominate the competition to such an extent that the clubhouse where the cup resided would come to be regarded as its permanent home. For well over a hundred years, Great Britain provided a succession of gallant but unsuccessful challengers although, from the outset, the New York Yacht Club declined any challenge unless it came from a Club rather than an individual. | | After years of protracted correspondence and a certain amount of acrimony, the first official challenge came in 1870, at the start of what was to prove a golden decade for American yachting. Further challenges followed rapidly, in 1871, 1876, 1881 and 1885, but American boats from the New York Yacht Club continued to hold sway. Then, in 1886, Lieutenant William Henn, RN, of the Royal Northern Yacht Club, who was to endear himself to every American he met, not least because he was accompanied by his wife, the first woman to cross the Atlantic in a racing yacht, decided to try his hand with his boat Galatea. With a displacement of 158 tons, she was 102½ feet in length and carried 7,505 square feet of sail. To defend the challenge, the New York Yacht Club put up Mayflower owned by Colonel Charles Paine. Despite her comparable length at 100 feet overall, her displacement was significantly less at 110 tons though she sported considerably more canvas with 8,600 square feet. In the event, these differences proved crucial and, on 7th September 1886 - over the New York Yacht Club's usual course off Sandy Hook – Mayflower came in first 12 minutes and 2 seconds ahead of Galatea. In the second race on 11th September, Mayflower romped home again, winning by just short of half an hour (29mins. 9secs.), thereby negating the need for any further races, and the personable Mr Henn returned home empty-handed, leaving the legendary Cup still in American hands.

provenance: Anon. sale, Christie's, London, 11 May 2000, lot 517. | Private collection, UK. | | This painting depicts two American clippers; Sweepstakes and Wild Pigeon together on the Indian Ocean in the summer of 1854 outward bound from China to New York. A journey that they only completed together once in their careers. | | Wild Pigeon was built by George Raynes at Portsmouth, New Hampshire for Olyphant & Co. of New York with the intention for working for the China trade. She was launched on 31st July 1851 and registered at 991 tons, measuring 189 feet in length with a 40 foot beam. She had striking features of long sharp lines and a large sail plan, with one observer commenting that she was 'one of the most beautiful and jaunty ships afloat'. She became a popular ship for both cargo and passengers and proved to be a fast sailor, completing consistently good passages, especially under the helm of Captain Mayhew. In 1865 she was sold and by 1868 she was Spanish owned and named Bella Juana, later renamed Voladora and rigged as a barque. On 17th February 1892 she was abandoned at sea in sinking condition. | | Sweepstakes was built by D.A. Westervelt at New York for Chambers and Heiser and launched on 21st June 1853. With a design suited for speed she was registered at 1,735 tons and measured 235 feet in length with a 41 foot beam. Unfortunately, she was damaged during her launch but was quickly repaired to enter service running, first to San Francisco and then to Hong Kong and China ports. She completed her fastest passage in 1857 travelling from New York to Bombay in only 74 days. In 1862, Sweepstakes sustained severe damage when she became grounded on a reef in the Sunda Straits for ten hours. Consequently she was sold for breaking in situ.
subject_matter: American clippers, Sweepstakes, Wild Pigeon, Indian Ocean, sailing, ships, summer 1854, China, New York

provenance: With MacConnal Mason & Sons, Ltd., London. | Anon. sale, Phillips, London, 14 March 1983, lot 90. | Anon. sale, Sotheby's, London, 3 June 1987, lot 255. | Property of a Palm Beach Estate. | Anon. sale, Christie's, New York, 12 October 2011, lot 105. | Private collection, Montana, and thence by descent. | | The extreme clipper Young America was christened with the seemingly perfect name, being one of those ships employed to open up the Pacific coast of the United States in the wake of the California Gold Rush of 1849. The last vessel to be designed and built by the great William Webb of New York, she was widely considered to be his crowning achievement when she was launched in 1853. Constructed from the finest materials available, at a massive cost of $140,000, she was registered at 1,961 tons and measured 243 feet in length with a 43 foot beam. Indeed, her lines were so admired by all who saw her that it was said she "was not excelled by anything afloat." | | Owned initially by the prominent New York merchant George B. Daniels, her size and speed ensured she commanded the highest freight rates and she never lacked cargo throughout her long career. Even in an era when many clippers and their captains were household names, she remained a favourite amongst shippers and over the course of twenty return passages from New York to San Francisco she averaged 118 days out and 98 back, both being well below the norm for the time. In 1872-73 she established the record of 82 days from the Golden Gate to New York, the fastest time ever recorded by a cargo-carrying sailing ship on that run. She also established a westbound record passage of 99 days from San Francisco to Liverpool, her other frequent destination, and as the years passed, she could be found in many ports across the Pacific with a wide variety of cargo. Sold out of American registry to Austrian owners in 1883, she was renamed Miroslav and adopted the Croatian port of Bakar as her homeport. Despite this, she continued in the trans-Atlantic trade until 1886 when, after leaving Delaware on 17th February, she disappeared without trace and was never heard of again.

provenance: With the Polak Mandell's Gallery, Jersey. | George Murray (friend of the artist who served in the Royal Naval Reserve; purchased from the above on 7th September 1985). | | A typed note on the artist's label reads: | | 'The 74-gun Ships-of-the-Line Ajax and Defiance, with a brig-sloop in company off the eastern end of the Isle of Wight in 1804. The nearer ship, the Ajax, was built on the Thames and completed in 1798. She took part in Calder's action with the French in 1805 and later the same year was one of the fleet which defeated the combined fleet of France and Spain off Cape Trafalgar on 21 October 1805.' | | Accompanying the work is a letter from Gardner to George Murray, dated 5 October 1985. In it Gardner writes about his delight in discovering that his old friend of over 50 years had purchased one of his paintings. He also provides some additional information about the painting that reads: | | 'A little background to the painting will interest you. The date is 1804 when both ships were part of the Channel Fleet. The Defiance was at that time commanded by Captain Philip Durham and the Ajax by Captain Wm Brown. The former fought his ship the following year in Sir Robert Calder's with the French in the Bay of Biscay and a few weeks later at Trafalgar. He was later knighted (KCB) and became a Rear Admiral. The Ajax was in Calder's action too but, as you may know, he was court martialled for incomptence[sic] and Captain Brown had to go home as a witness at Calder's court martial and so, to his great regret, was not present in the Ajax when she fought at Trafalgar in October 1805. | | The painting shows the two ships, with a brig in company off the eastern end of the Isle of Wight becalmed after leaving the anchorage off St. Helens.'

provenance: With Stevens Fine Art, Arizona. | Private collection, Switzerland. | | H.M.S. Pegasus – as she became known – was one of those innumerable vessels intended for a different purpose but, prior to completion, purchased by the Admiralty for service in the Great War. Laid down in John Brown's yard on Clydebank early in 1914, work on her was suspended when War broke out and she lay unfinished 'on the stocks' until bought by the Royal Navy in February 1917 for conversion into an aircraft and seaplane carrier. | | She had been ordered for the Great Eastern Railway Company's fleet to operate on its busy Harwich - the Hook of Holland ferry service and had been designed accordingly. Powered by steam turbines to give her a cruising speed of 20 knots, she was 332 feet in length with a 43 foot beam and was the last in a quartet of identical steamers, the other three already in use. When purchased, she was still bearing her christened name of Stockholm and was launched with it, but was re-named Pegasus soon afterwards. She was in service for the final year of the War and proved an invaluable addition to the fleet carrying, as she did, both fighter as well as floatplanes. Although not involved in any active combat, she spent 1918 supporting the Grand Fleet before being sent into the Russian White Sea to support the British operations against the Bolsheviks during 1919-20. Thereafter allotted to the Mediterranean Fleet, she was placed in reserve in 1925 and scrapped in 1931. By the time she was broken up, she had become obsolete and completely eclipsed by the more familiar type of modern aircraft carrier, but she was nevertheless a remarkable pioneer in the development of air power at sea when first deployed.
